newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM says Khmer Rouge leader forms new party.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM says Khmer Rouge leader forms new party.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Monday said a senior Khmer Rouge hardliner was forming a new political party that would support the prince's own political alliance.

"(Nominal Khmer Rouge leader) Khieu Samphan wants to set up a party called the Khmer Solidarity Party, without (top hardliners) Pol Pot, Ta Mok, and Son Sen," Ranariddh said at the opening of a primary school in the central province of Kompong Thom.
"He (Khieu Samphan) said he supports the 14-point platform of the National United Front," Ranariddh added.

The prince offered Khieu Samphan a "very great welcome" to his NUF alliance, which includes his royalist FUNCINPEC party, the opposition Khmer Nation Party and a wing of the small Buddhist Liberal Democratic Party (BLDP).
Ranariddh's announcement, if true, could mean he was ready to join political forces with the highest ranking member yet from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla movement, analysts said.
Analysts said such a move would also step up the prince's rivalry with co-Premier Hun Sen, with whom he had competed to recruit Khmer Rouge support.
Ranariddh and co-Premier Hun Sen, who rule the country in an uneasy coalition, have each added former guerrillas to their ranks since last August, when the rebels began defecting to the government.
In their bid to gain power, the leaders have given new political strength to the Khmer Rouge and formed what some outraged Cambodians have characterized as unholy alliances.
Ranariddh told villagers he had received the news about Khieu Samphan through Khmer Rouge contacts in the Kompong Thom district of Phnom Santuk.
The prince, a tape of whose speech was heard by Reuters, said Khieu Samphan had not objected to a NUF platform point that refers to the 1975-1979 Khmer Rouge government as a "genocidal regime."
The Khmer Rouge's clandestine radio did not mention the political party or NUF in its daily news segment.
Hun Sen, meanwhile, stressed on Monday that the Khmer Rouge regime must not be allowed to return to power.
He warned, in a speech aired on radio, that if the government did not remain alert the Khmer Rouge could return to power through political rather than military means.

The Khmer Rouge, which governed Cambodia by terror during its 1975-79 "killing fields" rule, signed a United Nations-brokered peace pact in 1991. The guerrillas later reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition government formed in 1993.

The movement has been decimated by the defections of thousands of fighters since former top official Ieng Sary split with hardliners last August and joined the government. Military analysts believe there are fewer than 2,000 fighters left, mostly in the north. SC KR LD
